title: India's Retail Investors Just Blinked. Equity Fund Inflows Crashed 40% in May.
excerpt: The sharpest monthly drop in a year has arrived, and Bernstein warns that SIP investors — the market's last line of defence — may not wait much longer for returns that have stopped coming.
body:
The money is getting nervous. Inflows into India's equity mutual funds plunged 40% month-on-month to ₹22,908 crore in May — the lowest level in twelve months — as the Iran war, $100-a-barrel crude, and persistent foreign selling finally shook the confidence of the country's retail investors.

The data, released by the Association of Mutual Funds in India on Wednesday, confirmed what market watchers had feared: the domestic investor, who had been single-handedly holding up the market against a wall of foreign outflows, is starting to pull back.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

Every major category bled. Small-cap fund inflows fell 28.2%, mid-cap fell 33.2%, and large-cap dropped 36.9%. Flexi-cap funds held up best with ₹5,175 crore in net inflows, but even that was a fraction of recent months. Hybrid scheme inflows halved to ₹10,560 crore. Debt funds recorded outflows of ₹96,949 crore. The mutual fund industry as a whole saw a net outflow of ₹64,131 crore in May.

Gold exchange-traded funds, which had been a safe haven through the crisis, recorded their first outflows in a year at ₹725 crore, as investors booked profits after the government's import duty hike to 15% pushed domestic gold prices higher even as global prices softened.

The industry's total assets under management slipped to ₹81.58 lakh crore from ₹81.92 lakh crore a month earlier.

"The lower inflows is due to extreme volatility in the markets as crude hovers around $100 a barrel, which has prompted near-term caution among investors," said Venkat Chalasani, CEO of AMFI.

## SIPs Are Still Standing — Barely

Systematic investment plans, the autopilot mechanism that has turned millions of Indians into disciplined equity investors, held above the ₹30,000 crore mark at ₹30,954 crore in May. But that was down from ₹31,115 crore in April, the second consecutive monthly decline. Contributing SIP accounts slipped to 9.64 crore from 9.65 crore. The gap between live SIP accounts (10.46 crore) and contributing accounts suggests a growing number of investors are hitting the pause button.

New SIP registrations stood at 54.16 lakh, while 51.70 lakh accounts were closed or matured — a narrowing margin that should concern the industry.

## Bernstein's Warning

Brokerage Bernstein added a dose of cold water. In a report released this week, it warned that investor patience is not infinite. Nearly one in three SIP investors surveyed said they would reassess their allocations within three to twelve months if returns remain flat. Another 17% said they could wait up to two years — but not longer.

The uncomfortable truth: several SIP vintages over the past one to two years have delivered flat or negative returns. For an investor who started a SIP in early 2025, the Nifty 50 is now 10.6% lower for the year and 11% below its peak. That is a hard pill when the narrative has been that SIPs smooth out volatility.

Bernstein also flagged a divergence between regular-plan investors, who get advice from distributors, and direct-plan investors, who tend to be more cost-conscious and more sensitive to returns. Fund houses relying heavily on direct-plan flows may see sharper volatility in their inflows during weak phases.

## The Foreign Selling Machine

Behind the domestic pullback is an even bigger force: foreign institutional investors have sold Indian shares worth $3.45 billion in May alone and have offloaded a record $30 billion in 2026. The rotation out of India — towards AI-heavy markets like Taiwan and South Korea, and into safer havens — shows no signs of slowing.

For the 30 million-plus NRIs and OCIs who invest in Indian mutual funds through SIPs, the message is nuanced. SIPs remain the most disciplined wealth-building mechanism available. But the macro environment — a war that is not ending, crude above $90, a rupee under pressure, and an RBI that may be forced to hike rates — demands a harder look at asset allocation. The era of set-it-and-forget-it may need a temporary pause for thought, even if the SIP itself should not pause.

**Sources:** Reuters, AMFI, The Hindu Business Line, Outlook Money, Bernstein Research
